item.content:encoded:
Why VMware Memory Tiering is not just swapping to NVMe

Memory is one of the most expensive resources in the data center, and workloads keep asking for more of it. We pack more VMs onto each host to get the most out of the hardware investment, but DRAM has a ceiling, both physical and financial. When memory runs short, the question comes up. Is Memory Tiering just swapping to NVMe?

We get this question a lot. Swapping is the boat is sinking. Memory Tiering is let’s steer away from that iceberg so we don’t sink. One is a desperate scramble after the fact. The other is a deliberate course correction before you hit trouble.

What swapping actually does

Swapping has been around for a long time. When a host runs out of memory and needs to reclaim some fast, the hypervisor picks pages and writes them out to disk to make room. It is a last resort, the equivalent of bailing water over the side because the hull has already been breached. The goal is correctness, keeping the system running when memory is exhausted.

The catch is that swapping does not care which pages it moves. A hot page that your application needs in the next millisecond can get swapped out right alongside a cold page that nobody has touched since boot. When that hot page is needed again, it has to be read back from disk, and performance takes a hit. You are bailing blindly, throwing important cargo overboard along with the ballast.

How Memory Tiering works differently

Broadcom, through its portfolio of VMware products, introduced Memory Tiering in VMware Cloud Foundation to extend host memory using NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) devices alongside traditional DRAM (dynamic random access memory). The result is a single logical memory space that VMs consume without knowing or caring which tier their pages live on, transparent to your applications.

Memory Tiering does not wait for a crisis. It runs continuously in the background, scanning VM memory pages in batches and classifying them as hot or cold using two signals. Recency tells us how recently a page was accessed. Frequency tells us how often it gets accessed. Hot pages stay in Tier 0, which is DRAM. Cold pages migrate to Tier 1, which is NVMe.

This is the core difference. Swap uses a simplistic random selection of pages. Memory Tiering uses sophisticated page aging techniques that classify pages by recency and frequency before deciding where they belong. Only cold pages move to NVMe, and hot pages stay in DRAM, with a small CPU footprint of roughly an eighth of a core on smaller hosts. Swap can touch any memory pages, including kernel memory under extreme conditions, but Memory Tiering only applies to VM memory pages, so the hypervisor itself always runs on fast DRAM.

Memory Tiering starts considering page movement when a threshold is reached. That threshold is not a fixed number. It is computed based on several conditions, including the current memory state, which in turn depends on minFree. minFree is not the amount of free memory on the host at a given moment. It is a computed target the VMkernel maintains as a safety buffer, derived from a sliding scale based on host memory size. The configuration of your hosts, the workloads running on them, and other variables all feed into where that line gets drawn. You might wonder why it waits for a threshold at all if it is supposed to be proactive. We want to keep most pages in DRAM as long as we can, because DRAM is where performance lives. The threshold is not a crisis point. It is spotting the iceberg on the horizon and adjusting course early, while there is still plenty of open water. The system is not fighting for resources. It is making a planned decision about page placement while there is still headroom.

From that point on, the tiering algorithm monitors page activity across both tiers and moves pages between DRAM and NVMe as workloads change. It moves cold pages to NVMe. Not hot pages, the way swap does. The pages your applications actually need stay right where they belong, in fast DRAM.

A practical example

Say you have a host with 1 TB of DRAM and 1 TB of NVMe configured for Memory Tiering. One of the VMs on it is a database server with a 512 GB memory allocation. The database has an active working set of about 200 GB that it accesses constantly. The remaining 312 GB holds cached data and rarely accessed buffers.

Without Memory Tiering, all 512 GB sits in DRAM, and you are paying for expensive memory that is mostly idle. With Memory Tiering, the hypervisor identifies the 200 GB working set as hot and keeps it in DRAM. The 312 GB of cold cache pages gradually migrates to NVMe. Your database still performs well because the pages it actually needs are in fast DRAM.

Now imagine the same scenario with swapping instead. The host hits memory pressure, and the hypervisor starts moving random pages to disk. Some might be part of the active working set, so the database stalls waiting for disk reads. You waited until the hull was taking on water, and now you are bailing out the good cargo along with the bad.

What this means in practice

This is where looking into your workload patterns pays off. Memory Tiering performs well when your active memory fits within your DRAM capacity. The default configuration uses a 1-to-1 DRAM-to-NVMe ratio, up to a maximum of 4 TB of NVMe tiering capacity. If your workloads have a lot of cold memory, which many do, you can extend your effective memory capacity significantly.

By placing cold pages on NVMe instead of buying more DRAM, you lower your total cost of ownership (TCO) per VM without sacrificing performance for the workloads that matter. You also get more consolidation, which means fewer hosts to power, cool, and manage. That translates to headroom for growth without a proportional jump in hardware spend.

The bottom line

If you have been thinking of Memory Tiering as just fancy swapping, give it a closer look. Pair it with the right NVMe drives and a sensible sizing strategy, and you get memory capacity and performance without choosing between them. Check out the Memory Tiering documentation for VMware Cloud Foundation to see how to configure it on your hosts, and start small with a 1-to-1 ratio to see the difference for yourself. The iceberg is a lot easier to avoid when you can see it coming.

item.content:encoded:
(Day 18 of 22 in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series. Today: VM security features)

Most of this series so far has focused on the infrastructure itself: hardware, hosts, management, and the networks in between. The virtual machines running on that infrastructure have security features of their own, though. Many of them sit unused simply because a VM was built from an old template, migrated from an older platform, or created in a hurry.

VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) gives every virtual machine the same kinds of protections that modern physical servers have: UEFI firmware, Secure Boot, a TPM, virtualization-based security, and encryption. Let’s go through them and take a look.

Build VM Security on UEFI and Secure Boot

Everything else in this post builds on UEFI firmware. Legacy BIOS firmware can’t do Secure Boot, can’t host a virtual TPM, and can’t run virtualization-based security, so the first step is making sure VMs use EFI firmware.

Secure Boot checks the signatures on the boot loader, kernel, and drivers before they load, which helps keep out malware that tries to hide underneath the operating system. It needs EFI firmware, virtual hardware version 13 or later, and a guest operating system that supports it. The VM has to be powered off to turn it on. The VCF Security Configuration Guide treats it as a top VM security priority.

A few things to know:

  • Converting from BIOS to UEFI takes work. Broadcom’s guidance for VMs that use virtualization-based security is to reinstall the guest (VBS best practices). Microsoft’s MBR2GPT tool can convert Windows 10 and 11 system disks in place (Microsoft), but test it, and take a snapshot first.
  • Secure Boot depends on updates. Secure Boot relies on lists of trusted and revoked signatures. The BlackLotus bootkit got around Secure Boot by loading older, vulnerable boot managers that were still validly signed, and the NSA’s guidance for mitigating it notes that virtual machines are affected, too (NSA). Keeping guests patched keeps those lists current.
  • Microsoft’s 2011 Secure Boot certificates are being replaced. Several Microsoft certificates that Secure Boot relies on expire in 2026. VMs keep booting, but VMs created on older versions of ESX, and the templates they came from, may not accept future Secure Boot updates until their certificates are refreshed. VCF raises a vCenter alarm for VMs that need the update and can update many of them automatically, and Broadcom’s guidance walks through the rest (KB 423893). You need to be running VCF 9.1.1 or a future vSphere 8.0 update, as well as VMware Tools 13.1.5 or newer, for these alarms and helpers to be present.

Give Windows a Virtual TPM

A virtual TPM (vTPM) is a software TPM 2.0 device that gives a VM the same kind of protected key storage that a physical TPM gives a physical server. Windows 11 requires a TPM 2.0 (Microsoft), and Windows uses it for BitLocker, Windows Hello, measured boot, and more.

A vTPM needs EFI firmware, virtual hardware version 14 or later, and a key provider, because its secrets are stored in the VM’s NVRAM file, which VM encryption protects. The Native Key Provider is enough, and with a vTPM, the standard resilience features, like vMotion, HA, and DRS, continue to work (vTPM overview). Our post on key provider design covers the keys.

Three details trip people up:

  • A vTPM doesn’t encrypt the virtual disks. Adding one encrypts the VM’s home files, like NVRAM and swap, and vCenter shows the VM as encrypted. The disks stay as they were, though, unless you also apply VM encryption, run atop an encrypted vSAN datastore, or use BitLocker inside the guest (vTPM overview). All of these things are compatible with vTPM-enabled VMs, too.
  • Clones copy the vTPM by default. Cloning a VM with a vTPM offers the choice of duplicating its TPM identity and secrets (the default, to match historical behavior) or replacing the vTPM with a blank copy. Replacing it destroys anything sealed to the old one, such as BitLocker keys, so suspend BitLocker first (KB 452119). Templates deserve special attention here, where you probably want to replace the vTPM.
  • Encrypted VMs can’t be exported as OVF or OVA files. That includes VMs with a vTPM, so keep their templates in a content library as VM templates. You can also use an OVF template with a vTPM placeholder, which gives each VM deployed from it a new vTPM with its own secrets (tech docs).

Turn On Virtualization-Based Security

Virtualization-based security (VBS) is a Windows feature that uses the hypervisor built into Windows to wall off a region of memory from the rest of the operating system. Windows uses it for Credential Guard, which protects credentials like NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets from theft (Microsoft), and for memory integrity, also called HVCI, which makes it much harder to load malicious code into the kernel (Microsoft). Newer versions of Windows turn Credential Guard on by default when the hardware supports it, so turning on VBS in the VM may be most of the work.

In VCF, VBS is a checkbox in the VM’s settings, and you then turn on the features you want inside Windows (VBS best practices). You don’t need to install the Hyper-V role in the guest, because Windows handles that itself. It needs EFI firmware and Secure Boot, along with virtual hardware version 14 or later on Intel hosts, or 19 or later on AMD hosts. Plan for the trade-offs:

  • Some features don’t mix with VBS. Fault Tolerance, PCI passthrough (which also impacts how GPUs might be consumed), and hot-adding CPU or memory aren’t supported on VBS-enabled VMs.
  • Performance depends on the CPU. Memory integrity runs best on newer processors with hardware support for it, where the overhead tends not to be noticeable and is worth the trade-off even when it is, but test with your own workloads.
  • Drivers matter. Memory integrity can block incompatible drivers, so test before rolling it out widely.

VBS walls are built by the guest’s own hypervisor, which runs on top of ESX, so VBS doesn’t protect a guest from someone who controls the host; Microsoft says as much about memory integrity. Protecting a VM’s memory from the host is a job for confidential computing.

Choose Where to Encrypt

Physical servers usually get disk encryption from the operating system, like BitLocker on Windows or LUKS on Linux, with keys protected by the server’s TPM. VMs with a vTPM can work the same way. In VCF, though, encrypting inside every guest usually isn’t necessary. vSAN data-at-rest encryption encrypts every VM’s disks without any changes to the guests and keeps vSAN’s compression and deduplication savings. Our post on storage encryption covers this, along with VM encryption for other storage.

vSAN encryption protects the data on the drives, but it’s transparent to anything that reads through the hypervisor, so someone who can clone a VM or download its files through vCenter gets readable data. Encrypting inside the guest adds a layer against that for the VMs that hold the keys to everything else, like domain controllers, certificate authorities, and secrets vaults. For those:

  • Give them a vTPM. BitLocker protects its keys with a TPM, and LUKS can, too, so give guests that encrypt their disks a vTPM, just as you’d give a physical server a TPM.
  • Add a BitLocker pre-boot PIN for the most critical VMs. Someone with enough privileges in vCenter can clone a VM and start the copy, and because the clone gets a copy of the vTPM, BitLocker unlocks it, too, unless it needs a PIN at startup. The PIN has to be entered after every restart, so save it for systems like domain controllers, where that operational trade-off is worth it.
  • Control who can decrypt, and who can copy. Encryption only helps if the people who shouldn’t see the data also don’t hold the cryptographic privileges. So give most administrators the built-in No Cryptography Administrator role and keep cryptographic privileges with a small group (docs). Privileges that copy a VM, like cloning, exporting, and downloading files from a datastore, deserve the same care.
  • Weigh the costs. Data encrypted inside the guest doesn’t compress or deduplicate, on vSAN or in your backup system. Every guest also needs its own recovery keys, stored somewhere you can reach when that VM is down, and for domain controllers, that shouldn’t be only the Active Directory they serve. The encryption also uses some guest CPU, so double-encrypting data on disk needs to be tested and thought through.

VM Security Settings: What’s Already Done and What to Change

Older hardening guides were full of VM settings to change. Many of those are now the defaults, and the VCF Security Configuration Guide lists them so you can audit them instead of setting them again. Copy, paste, and drag-and-drop between the console and the guest are off, as are disk shrinking, disk wiping, and connecting or disconnecting devices from inside the guest, and guests can’t read details about the host they run on. If you find any of them turned back on, find out why.

A handful of VM security settings still need changing:

  • Limit console connections. Set RemoteDisplay.maxConnections to 1, so nobody can watch an administrator’s session through a second console connection. Keep in mind, though, that if your session is disconnected via network instability you might have to wait until it times out to reconnect.
  • Lock the console on disconnect. For Windows guests, set tools.guest.desktop.autolock to TRUE, so closing the console doesn’t leave a logged-in session for the next person.
  • Boot only from disk. Set bios.bootDeviceClasses to allow:hd, and allow the CD drive only while you’re installing an operating system.
  • Remove hardware you don’t use. Every virtual device is code that a guest can talk to. When a critical vulnerability turned up in virtual USB controllers, the workaround was removing USB controllers from VMs (VMSA-2024-0006). Test first, because some devices are less optional than they look; removing the USB controller can affect console input in some guests, for example.
  • Keep virtual hardware current. The guide recommends hardware version 17 or later. Newer virtual hardware versions have performance and security improvements, as well as better compatibility with new physical hardware.
  • Set encrypted vMotion to Required for sensitive VMs. The default, Opportunistic, already encrypts migrations whenever both hosts support it, which current hosts do, and Required makes sure a migration is never sent in the clear (docs). Adding a vTPM or VM encryption switches a VM to Required automatically. Set encrypted Fault Tolerance to Required, too, for VMs that use it.

Lock Down VMware Tools

VMware Tools matters for VM security, too, and it has security settings of its own in each guest’s tools.conf file. The VCF Security Configuration Guide covers them, and you can change each one with the VMwareToolboxCmd utility that comes with Tools, as in “VMwareToolboxCmd config set guestoperations disabled true”, or by editing tools.conf. These are the ones to change:

  • Turn off guest operations where you don’t need them. Guest operations let vCenter run commands, move files, and list processes inside a guest. This makes them handy for automation and just as handy for an attacker who gets into vCenter. Many backup, disaster recovery, and automation tools depend on them, so check first, and leave them on in templates, because guest customization needs them.
  • Prevent re-customization of deployed VMs. Guest customization can run scripts as root or Administrator, so someone with access to vCenter could use it on a deployed VM to reset the Administrator password or add an account of their own. Set deployPkg enable-customization to false once a VM is deployed, unless something like a disaster recovery plan uses customization to change its IP address. Leave it on in templates, or the VMs you deploy from them won’t customize.
  • Turn off inventory features you don’t use. Application, service, and container discovery (appinfo, servicediscovery, and containerinfo) report what’s running in a guest to vCenter, where tools like VCF Operations use the data for application monitoring and dependency mapping. Leave them on where you use that data, and turn them off everywhere else.
  • Keep upgrades from changing features. Set autoupgrade allow-add-feature and allow-remove-feature to false, so automatic upgrades patch the Tools features you have without adding or removing any. Set gueststoreupgrade policy to off unless you deliver Tools upgrades through GuestStore.
  • Send Tools logs to the guest’s system log. Set the Tools logging handlers to syslog, which routes Tools activity to syslog on Linux and the event log on Windows, so whatever already ships the guest’s logs picks it up, too.
  • Keep VMware Tools current. It’s software like any other, and our post on patching applies to it, too. Linux distributions ship open-vm-tools, which updates with the rest of the guest’s packages, and for Windows, leave automatic Tools upgrades on unless you update Tools another way.

A few Tools settings are already where the guide wants them, like GlobalConf, which can push tools.conf changes to guests from a central source and is off by default, so audit those. The guide’s PowerCLI scripts audit and remediate the VM settings in the previous section and check whether Tools is current (tools). But tools.conf lives inside each guest, so set these with the configuration management you already use for the guest operating system.

Make VM Security Features the Default

The easiest VM security is the kind nobody has to remember. Build these features into your templates and content libraries: EFI firmware, Secure Boot, a current hardware version, a vTPM for Windows, VBS where the workload supports it, unneeded devices removed, and the recommended Tools settings in place. Leave guest operations and customization on, though, because templates need them. New VMs then start out with these protections in place, and the work shifts to the VMs that already exist.

For those, start your VM security work with the VMs that matter most, like domain controllers, certificate authorities, secrets vaults, and anything else an attacker would love to copy, and work outward from there. Every VM you bring up to date is one less easy target.

item.content:encoded:
Years ago, a new backup product came to market. The product name featured the words “Backup and Restore.” I remember asking one of their salespeople, “Isn’t that kind of wordy?” He turned and asked me, “Yes, but have you used backup products that ONLY have backup in the name…and did the restores always work?”

He had a point. Before modern backup APIs, file-based backups didn’t always capture system state. Image-based backups of entire systems were often complicated, expensive, and relatively rare. Restores could involve long incremental chains, feeding tapes one by one. Backups would happily fail for weeks or months if nobody read the reports every morning. Often, we were recovering one failed server, with VSS, secondary copies, and application-level recovery providing a safety net for a missing backup. Modern, coordinated encryption and destruction of data by advanced ransomware operators have changed that threat landscape. Complete backups and working restores matter more than ever. Part of assessing your ransomware response posture is making sure you have fast, reliable recovery from backups that are protected and separated from production. What does this require?

Start with copies an attacker cannot take with them

The familiar 3-2-1 rule is a useful starting point: three copies of your data, on two types of media, with one copy offsite. It forces you to think beyond the production datastore. Three folders on the same storage system do not accomplish the same thing.

Ransomware adds another question: can someone who compromises production also delete your recovery copies? Offsite helps with a building failure. It does less for you if the same compromised administrator account controls both sites. Protect recovery infrastructure with separate administrative access, appropriate network boundaries, and offline or immutable copies. CISA’s ransomware guidance explicitly calls for offline backups and regular recovery testing.

A local snapshot remains useful, but losing the datastore can take it with the VM. As I covered in Snapshots Are Your Best Friend, remote protection belongs alongside local recovery options.

Make restore testing routine

A backup job reporting success tells you that the backup software finished its job. You still need to find out whether the application works.

Automate recovery into an isolated “bubble” network on hardware separated from production. VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) networking can provide the overlay networks and policies to build that environment. Configure and test the isolation explicitly, including outbound access; creating another network segment alone does not make it a clean room. Restored copies should not register themselves in production DNS, send customer emails, or start processing the same payment queue as the live application.

Then test beyond power-on. Can users authenticate? Does the database recover? Can the application complete a representative transaction? Record the restore point, results, and elapsed time, and rerun the tests as the application changes. A booting VM is a useful milestone. A working service is the recovery objective. A server that has a corrupt bootloader will back up fine, but it will not restore fine, and the only way to know recovery is possible is regular testing. 

Find a restore point you can trust

The newest backup may contain encrypted data. An older one may contain the attacker’s foothold. Immutability preserves a restore point; it does not establish that the contents are clean.

This is where the cyber-recovery capabilities in VCF Protection and Recovery, previously VMware Live Recovery, become useful. Guided restore-point selection and behavioral analysis help teams evaluate candidate recovery points in an isolated environment before returning workloads to service. VMware’s overview explains that workflow. VCF 9.1 also supports a customer-managed, on-premises clean room with the VMware Advanced Cyber Compliance add-on, including isolation and EDR integration. The vSAN Protection and Recovery overview covers the on-premises option.

Give the security team time and space to examine candidates, remediate vulnerabilities, and address compromised credentials. A malware scan is evidence for that decision, not a guarantee that every trace of an intrusion has disappeared.

Keep enough history without making the vault unaffordable

If you discover an intrusion today, yesterday’s copy may already be too recent. Recovery history needs to reach back far enough to give you useful choices.

A vSAN cyber vault can provide the protected storage behind that process. vSAN ReadyNodes certified for cyber recovery support high-density QLC flash, giving recovery environments a more economical all-flash capacity option. Global deduplication in vSAN ESA, generally available in VCF 9.1, can reduce duplicate blocks across the cluster. Actual savings depend on the data; data already compressed or encrypted inside the guest or application will offer fewer opportunities.

Size for retained history, incoming changes, and the working space needed to validate recovery candidates. The vault needs room for the investigation as well as the copies. Use certified hardware and account for QLC endurance and the supported recovery use case when selecting a profile.

Put the critical applications on a fast recovery path

Restoring one accidentally deleted file and restoring the business are very different storage workloads. A repository that comfortably absorbs overnight backups may struggle when hundreds of VMs need to read from it at once.

Tape and capacity-focused magnetic storage can still have a place in the retention strategy. But if your critical application has a four-hour recovery objective, discovering that its restore takes 17 hours is a design failure you want to find during a test. Watching a large restore crawl along is like watching paint dry, except someone from the business keeps asking whether it is dry yet.

Keep your most critical services on a recovery path that can meet their objectives. Flash-resident replicas and recovery points can avoid some of the delays of retrieving and reconstructing data from slower tiers. Test the whole path, though: network throughput, concurrent restores, security validation, application startup, and dependencies all consume time. Fast storage helps; it does not turn an untested runbook into a four-hour recovery plan.

Recover foundational services such as identity, DNS, and key management in the order the applications actually need them. Measure success when the service is usable. You do not want storage throughput to become the reason the business starts entertaining an attacker’s sales pitch.

Have somewhere to recover that is not the crime scene

Your recovery plan needs a destination that the incident has not compromised. That might be a separate customer-owned environment or a VMware-powered cloud service provider. Confirm the capacity, access, connectivity, and recovery procedures before you need them.

The recovery compute does not necessarily have to sit idle all year. A suitably isolated, general-purpose cluster could run lower-priority test/dev workloads during normal operation. The runbook can specify which workloads shut down to free capacity, who can authorize that decision, and how critical recovered services receive priority.

Use vSphere resource pools, reservations, and DRS deliberately, and test the plan under contention. Shares control relative access to resources; they do not create capacity, and their effect depends on the resource-pool hierarchy. Keep the vault and clean-room security boundaries intact even when you share compute. A QLC recovery-storage profile and the compute needed to run production applications are separate sizing and support decisions.

Pick a critical application and walk the entire recovery path: select a protected copy, validate it in isolation, recover its dependencies, and have the application owner prove it works. Record how long it took and fix what slowed it down. That is how recovery becomes another working layer of your defense in depth.

The backup report can tell you what was copied last night. The restore test tells you whether you can bring the business back.

item.content:encoded:
Multi-Tenancy Is the Engine of the Modern Private AI Cloud

The private cloud is undergoing a profound transformation. Today’s enterprise IT organizations are tasked with supporting diverse, resource-intensive workloads, spanning AI, Kubernetes / containers, and virtual machines, on shared infrastructure. Simultaneously, they must enforce strict isolation between business divisions, developers, or external clients. When isolation relies on manual administrative processes, IT teams can expect configuration drift, security vulnerabilities, sluggish provisioning, and wasted resources. To build a true cloud ecosystem rather than merely bolting self-service portals onto static infrastructure, multi-tenancy is a critical necessity.

Enter VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9, a platform that enables enterprises to establish a fully governed, multi-tenant private AI cloud aligned with how modern applications are built. Written for IT executives, cloud architects, platform engineers, and administrators, our new whitepaper focuses on the “why” and “what” of multi-tenancy, highlighting the business problems it solves rather than deep implementation details. By explaining why multi-tenancy matters now, how VCF Automation delivers it, and what makes it different, the paper shows how IT can provide secure, self-service consumption while maintaining strong control.

Here’s a preview of the core architectural concepts and business outcomes of a multi-tenant private AI cloud explored in the full whitepaper.

A Kubernetes-Native Foundation for All Apps

VCF 9 reimagines multi-tenancy by rooting it in a Kubernetes-based architecture. At its core lies the VMware vSphere Supervisor, a Kubernetes-based control plane executing directly on vSphere clusters. This architecture drives the “All Apps” organization, exposing infrastructure and services through Kubernetes APIs and Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs). By utilizing a common declarative API surface, platform teams and developers can consume private cloud services, including KubeVM, VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS), container, networking, database services, and more efficiently.

Empowering the Provider and the Consumer

Multi-tenancy and self-service are fundamentally inseparable; delivering self-service without structural isolation can introduce security and governance risks. VCF Automation resolves this via a provider/consumer model that mirrors public cloud operations. Enterprise IT acts as the provider, managing the underlying fabric, allocating resources, and defining global security guardrails. Meanwhile, lines of business operate as tenants inside secure, autonomous boundaries. This dynamic operates on a concentric model: enterprise control sits at the outer ring, tenant autonomy and security guardrails form the middle ring, and frictionless developer consumption resides at the inner ring.

A cornerstone of this autonomy is the Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Tenants can self-provision isolated VPCs and subnets on demand. Furthermore, they retain direct control over Distributed Firewall policies and NAT configurations within their project boundaries. Supported by VMware vDefend, security mandates are strictly enforced in a sequential hierarchy from the top down, so that corporate rules cannot be bypassed by lower-level users.

Governing the Private AI Frontier

As enterprises scale Private AI, dedicating physical GPU infrastructure to individual teams quickly becomes cost-prohibitive. VCF Private AI Services facilitates multi-tenant model sharing, enabling the secure pooling and sharing of GPU resources across the organization. The Model Runtime permits the secure sharing of AI models between isolated namespaces. This maintains vital data privacy while helping avoid redundant model deployments that waste infrastructure allocation.

Advanced Capabilities and Use Cases for Enterprise Complexity

Our newly published whitepaper details how this architecture supports sophisticated enterprise requirements, unlocking advanced capabilities and use cases:

  • Multi-Tenant Disaster Recovery: The Protection and Recovery for VCF Automation service integrates disaster recovery natively into the multi-tenant framework. Tenants can self-serve VM-level replication without exhausting shared recovery capacity. Importantly, tenant isolation boundaries are continuously maintained across replication and failover phases.
  • Policy as Code: VCF Automation enforces governance through Kubernetes Validating Admission Policy, allowing administrators to apply granular YAML-based controls over IaaS resource provisioning.
  • App Stack Formation: Platform engineers can capture a running sandbox environment, including its network configurations, as a reusable blueprint. Teams can redeploy identical or differentiated copies of these complex application topologies to reduce configuration drift.

Maximizing ROI with Embedded FinOps

Resource hoarding drives inflated CapEx in private data centers. VCF Automation combats this with embedded FinOps capabilities powered with VCF Operations that provide granular, namespace-level cost accountability. Upfront pricing models influence user behavior, while automated lease policies and reclamation workflows systematically reclaim inactive resources. This helps ensure that idle capacity is reclaimed automatically and redistributed, significantly optimizing hardware utilization and reducing Total Cost of Ownership (TCO).

item.content:encoded:
Part 4 of 4: Governing the Agentic Loop – Bringing Platform as a Service and Governed Agentic Loop with Tanzu and AgentMinder

An AI agent needs more than a model. It needs instructions and skills, memory to retain context, and tools that let it interact with the systems around it. Every connection makes the agent more useful. Every connection also gives us another access decision to govern.

A marketing agent might need campaign data, a content library, and publishing tools. An infrastructure agent might need Kubernetes inventory and VMware Cloud Foundation management tools. Both can use the same underlying model, but they should have very different authority.
If you want to see the demo first, jump to the video at the end of this post where we go through the process of building an agent, controlling its bound services using a bind, controlling access to specific intents through a grant in AgentMinder and finally scrub PII form being processed on the agent itself. 

In Part 1, we established compute tenancy and network isolation. 

In Part 2, we applied VMware vDefend microsegmentation to control traffic between AI components. 

In Part 3, we added application-layer inspection with Avi WAF and authenticated, encrypted communication with Istio.

Those controls establish where traffic can travel and how we protect it. Now we need to govern what an agent can do through an allowed connection.

An authenticated agent can send a perfectly valid request over an encrypted channel and still ask for something outside its responsibilities. Counting virtual machines and changing a network may use the same infrastructure endpoint. The distinction has to be enforced above the IP address and port.

In this lab, we use Tanzu Platform and AgentMinder to demonstrate three controls within agentic governance: bind, grant, and scrub. We deploy an agent, connect its services, authorize specific groups of tools, and filter sensitive content on the model path.

What the Agent Needs: Skills, Memory, a Model, and Tools

The agentic loop starts with a request. The agent sends context to a model, selects a tool, examines the result, and decides whether another action is necessary before answering.

Several dependencies support that loop:

Instructions help the agent choose a sensible action. The platform and authorization layer enforce whether that action is allowed.

Our demo concentrates on the model and MCP connections. Skills and memory are in the same access model, but we are not demonstrating separate policy controls for each of them in this walkthrough.

MCP: A Door That Describes Its Tools

Model Context Protocol, or MCP, gives an agent a standard way to discover and invoke capabilities exposed by an endpoint, or a server.

Think of an MCP server as an active API doorway: it presents the available tools, explains what they do, and describes the arguments each tool accepts. The agent discovers those definitions through tools/list and invokes a selected tool through tools/call. The server’s implementation performs the underlying work. See the MCP tools specification.

Consider an infrastructure platform like VCF with thousands of API operations. We could point an agent directly at the environment, give it a username, password, and shell, and ask it to complete a task. The agent would then have to read the documentation, identify the right CLIs or APIs, work out the parameters, execute commands, interpret errors, and keep looping until it succeeds. That discovery and trial-and-error process can be slow, error-prone, and expensive in tokens. An MCP server gives the agent a structured starting point: a defined set of tools that wrap the underlying CLI commands and API calls, with descriptions and input schemas explaining how to invoke them. The agent selects the appropriate tool while the server handles the integration details, reducing repeated discovery and potentially cutting both token consumption and execution time. That tool interface also creates a doorway where we can enforce governance: which agent may invoke which tool, against which resources, and under what conditions.

Eight or ten tools could cover a focused workflow across thousands of APIs. Now, MCP requires a good design, enterprise implementation, rigorous testing and verification. Our VCF MCP catalog grew during the lab as we separated capabilities into more precise tools.

This makes the next question unavoidable: discovering a tool tells the agent what it can do. Who decides whether it is allowed to execute it?

The Lab Architecture: Two MCP Paths, Different Enforcement

We deploy the demo agent on Tanzu Platform, running on VCF. Avi provides the application ingress and WAF layer shown in the architecture, vDefend provides the L4 network segmentation preventing the agent from reaching any system directly. AgentMinder runs on a VKS cluster.

As you can see in the diagram below, the agent has three service connections:

  • A private LLM service.
  • A Kubernetes MCP service reached directly and not through agentminder.
  • A VCF MCP service reached through the local AgentMinder sidecar and AgentMinder gateway.

Figure 1. The agent runs on Tanzu. Kubernetes tool calls use a direct MCP connection, while VCF tool calls traverse the AgentMinder sidecar and gateway. Tanzu AI Services invokes the external PII filter on the model interaction path.

The two tool paths are deliberately different:

Agent → Kubernetes MCP → Kubernetes API

Agent → Local sidecar → AgentMinder gateway → VCF MCP → VCF APIs

Kubernetes provides our comparison case. It has no AgentMinder intent enforcement on this path. Only its MCP credentials and Kubernetes permissions apply.

VCF adds a separate additional authorization decision between connecting the service and executing a tool.

Runtime Containment: Control What the Agent Can Execute

Governance starts inside the container. Runtime containment means controlling the agent’s execution environment: the operating-system packages, binaries, libraries, credentials, and local tools available to it. We use a stripped-down container environment containing the dependencies the agent needs. Additional shells, administrative utilities, and installation privileges should be available only where the workload requires them. We use Tanzu buildpacks to assemble that environment during deployment, supplying the runtime and dependencies the agent needs from a platform-managed configuration. We test the resulting package and deploy it as an immutable artifact: updates go through a new build and deployment rather than changes to the running container. This gives platform teams a consistent, repeatable way to control what the agent runs.Together with controlled MCP access, this limits both the tools the agent can invoke remotely and the capabilities it can exercise locally.

Deny by Default: Control What the Agent Can Reach

At the network layer, we apply deny by default: explicitly allow the connections the workload needs and block the rest. This extends the Zero Trust segmentation approach we established with vDefend in Part 2. The agent should reach its approved model and tool endpoints without gaining a general route into management networks or unrelated services. On the governed VCF path, that means allowing access through AgentMinder while restricting the backend to the gateway. Runtime containment limits available capabilities; segmentation limits where those capabilities can be used.

First Control: Bind the Services the Agent Can Use

We start by pushing the prepared agent package to Tanzu:

cf push 

The package includes the sidecar configuration. On its initial deployment, the application can start without a model binding, but it cannot complete a useful conversation.

Next, we bind the model service (in the video it is done though the Apps Manager UI)

Before binding services to an agent, platform engineering teams must decide which MCP servers and services are made available. In a large enterprise, granting every agent access to all available services risks resource bloat and unnecessary exposure.

The Tanzu Platform Marketplace provides a self-service catalog that lets teams curate and expose only approved, organization-suitable services to agents. This upfront governance ensures agents consume appropriate infrastructure tiers without overwhelming backend resources, establishing a clear boundary before an application ever binds or invokes a service:

cf bind-service infrademo-agent private-ai-llm

cf restart infrademo-agent

The agent now has the model connection it needs to reason about requests.

This is the first governance boundary. Platform teams determine which services are available to an application and who can configure those bindings. A marketing agent receives its approved marketing services. An infrastructure agent receives its approved infrastructure services.

In our lab, we then bind the two MCP services:

cf bind-service infrademo-agent k8s-mcp-direct

cf bind-service infrademo-agent sc-infrademo-vcf

cf restart infrademo-agent

These commands use the lab’s service-instance names. The same bindings can be made in Apps Manager as it is done in the recorded demo.

Tanzu Platform’s bind-service associates the service instance with the application. In this deployment, restarting refreshes the application’s runtime environment so it can consume the new bindings. Under the hood, the binding makes the service’s connection details such as its endpoint and credentials available to the application through the VCAP_SERVICES environment variable. The agent reads those details to connect to the model or MCP service without hardcoding them into its source. 

In our lab the Kubernetes binding points directly to the Kubernetes MCP server at [KUBERNETES_MCP_URL], while the VCF binding points to the local AgentMinder sidecar at 127.0.0.1:8181. Notice the difference: Kubernetes tool calls go directly to the MCP server, bypassing AgentMinder. VCF tool calls pass through the sidecar and AgentMinder gateway, where the agent’s grants determine which tools it can execute. Think of a binding as giving the agent the service’s address and connection details which for the direct Kubernetes MCP, that connection lets the agent use the tools permitted by the service’s credentials. For VCF, the binding connects the agent through AgentMinder, where a separate grant determines which groups of tools it may use. The bind establishes the connection and the grant authorizes the actions. 

At this point, we have connected both services. We have not granted the demo agent a VCF intent.

Proving the Difference

We ask the agent a Kubernetes inventory question:

How many namespaces are in the Kubernetes cluster?

The request succeeds using the direct Kubernetes MCP path and its configured permissions.

Then we ask:

How many VMs do I have?

The VCF operation fails because the agent has no applicable grant.

The application is running. Its model works. The VCF service is bound. What is missing is authorization to perform the requested operation.

Second Control: Grant an Intent, Then Enforce It at Runtime

An AgentMinder intent is a grouping of tools around a defined job.

For this demo, we separate VM management from network management. VM tools belong to the first intent; network tools belong to the second. A grant authorizes an agent identity to use a corresponding intent.

That separation matters because a generic tool that accepts arbitrary API paths makes the boundary harder to enforce. If the same tool can list VMs, modify networks, and change storage, granting that tool may authorize far more than the intended job.

During the lab, we moved from broad operations toward explicit domain tool sets. VM management became a bundle of VM tools, making the scope of its grant visible and enforceable.

The word intent here refers to a configured authorization object. This does not mean that the agent can gain access to tools through its own prompts and requests. These are explicitly granted and enforced by AgentMinder.

Under the Hood: Identity, Bearer Tokens, and the Gateway

The demo agent has a registered AgentMinder identity. Its client configuration is available to the sidecar, which handles the authenticated connection on the agent’s behalf.

This is the identity and access layer. Tanzu controls who can deploy the application and configure its service bindings. AgentMinder identifies the calling agent and enforces which intents and tools that identity is authorized to use. A service binding establishes the configured connection; the grant determines the permitted operations on the governed path. Each agent therefore needs an identifiable, appropriately scoped identity so that access decisions can be attributed to the agent making the request.

The relevant request flow is:

  1. The agent selects a VCF tool and sends the request to the local sidecar.
  2. The sidecar obtains or reuses an access token for the configured agent identity.
  3. The sidecar presents that token to the AgentMinder gateway as a bearer token.
  4. The gateway evaluates the requested tool against its configured intent binding and the agent’s authorized scopes.
  5. An authorized call proceeds to the VCF MCP backend, which performs the corresponding infrastructure API operation. An unauthorized call is denied.

AgentMinder separates the administrative configuration of identities, intents, tool bindings, and grants from runtime gateway enforcement. Broadcom describes this gateway as the enforcement point for authenticated, authorized tool calls. See the AgentMinder announcement.

We now grant the demo agent VM management in AgentMinder and repeat:

How many VMs do I have?

The agent can invoke the VM inventory tool and answer from the returned data.

Then we ask:

How many networks do I have?

That operation remains denied. The agent is connected to the same MCP service, but the network tool belongs to an intent it has not been granted.

Finally, we grant network management and repeat the network question. The corresponding tool call can now succeed.

The demo uses inventory questions to make the boundary easy to observe. The configured VM management intent also included mutation capabilities, so it should not be described as a read-only grant. A production inventory agent could instead receive a narrower intent containing only read operations.

Discovery and Token Refresh Are Separate Concerns

Two implementation details affected this demonstration.

First, the agent’s displayed tool catalog and its execution permissions are separate. Seeing a tool in the interface does not prove that the agent can invoke it.

Second, updating a grant does not rewrite a token already cached by the sidecar. During testing, a token minted before authorization continued to carry its earlier scopes.

We configured a 60-second token lifetime for the demo identity and corrected the refresh handling used by the integration. That value is specific to the lab configuration. 

Closing the Direct Backend Path

There is one more connection between this post and the earlier infrastructure work.

If the gateway enforces tool authorization, an agent must not be able to bypass it by calling the MCP backend directly.

For the deployed architecture, backend reachability therefore needs to be restricted to the gateway through the applicable routing, firewall, and application-access controls.

This is where the layers reinforce each other. AgentMinder governs which tool calls are authorized. The network and platform controls make the enforced route the only available route. The demonstrated gateway behavior is not, by itself, proof that every alternative path has been closed.

Third Control: Scrub Sensitive Content on the Model Path

An agent can be authorized to use a service and still carry information that should not reach the model in its original form.

For the final demonstration, we use Tanzu AI Services webhooks to invoke an external PII scrubber built with Presidio. It could be any system that supports being called using a webhook.

This integration is separate from AgentMinder’s MCP authorization path. AgentMinder governs tool access. Tanzu AI Services provides the interception point for the content filter.

In the lab build, the AI Services Policy configuration exposed the webhook capability as a technical preview, enabled through webhook. The integration provided these endpoints:

/prompt

/response

/response/stream

Our pii-scrub application implements the filtering service. Presidio identified configured entities, and its anonymization functionality replaces detected values with labels. 

We submit a synthetic contact card and ask the agent to repeat its contents. The filter acts on the AI Services processing path as the model is replying that it cannot disclose personal information does not prove that the scrubber ran. 

The webhook model also provides an integration point for other content inspection services, including appropriately configured PHI or prompt-injection detection. Those require their own implementation and validation. Our lab demonstrates PII replacement.

Audit: Make Every Access Traceable

The Forth discipline is audit, and it spans the stack. Tanzu records endpoint access. AgentMinder records actions attempted through its gateway, including both allowed and denied requests. At the runtime and infrastructure layers, vDefend, Avi, and VCF/VKS provide the network, application-access, and platform audit records.

Together, these records let us trace which agent accessed a service, which operation it attempted, whether the gateway authorized it, and what happened along the underlying application and infrastructure path. Correlating those records gives us an end-to-end account of the agent’s activity, including attempts that were blocked before reaching the target system.

What This Means for Governed Agentic Coding

The same decisions apply to a coding agent.

It may need repository access, build tools, package sources, memory, and deployment services. Binding those services gives the runtime its configured dependencies. Grants can then separate inspection, testing, and deployment capabilities. Content inspection can govern sensitive information passing through the model service.

Our infrastructure demo makes those boundaries visible with VM and network questions. A development workflow can apply the same pattern to reviewing code, running a build, and deploying the result.

Across the four parts, we have assembled complementary controls: tenant isolation, network segmentation, application inspection, authenticated communication, service bindings, tool authorization, and content filtering.

Each answers a different question. Together, they let us build useful agents whose access is defined and enforced outside the model’s reasoning loop.

item.content:encoded:
In this blog, we explore a powerful new capability introduced in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1.1 which further enhances compliance and configuration management. Previously, VCF Operations offered Security Posture Management and Configuration Management only from the user interface.  

Now, admins have an option to manage compliance and configuration management with programmatic access via the API.  

To provide context, we will first walk through the various forms of Salt before introducing our latest enhancement: the VMware Salt for VCF components API.

The open-source Salt API: Where it starts

The open-source Salt Project is a free, community-driven configuration management and remote-execution tool that lets you manage infrastructure at scale. It ships with its own REST API that lets you programmatically trigger and run commands on remote systems, apply configuration states, and orchestrate tasks across nodes. This open-source API is the foundational layer for all Salt deployments. It provides powerful remote execution and state management. 

Open-source Salt is CLI-driven with limited built-in reporting, basic role-based access control configured using text files, and does not have a centralized UI by default. The open-source Salt API is best suited for teams that need raw Salt automation and are willing to build their own reporting, governance, and integrations around it.

How open-source Salt is built: The master–minion architecture

Under the hood, open-source Salt uses a master–minion architecture.

A Salt master is a service — a long-running process installed on a virtual machine or physical server — that acts as the central control node. It issues commands, stores configuration files, and coordinates work across the systems it manages. 

A Salt minion is a lightweight agent process installed on each individual endpoint (system) you want to manage — whether that’s a VM, physical server, network device or other devices. 

The minion receives instructions from the master and reports back results. The Salt master publishes jobs, and the Salt minions decide if the job is applicable to them. This architecture is simple and effective.  Each master operates independently – there is no built-in mechanism for tying multiple masters together into a unified, centrally managed system. This limitation is part of what VMware Salt (described below) is designed to address.

VMware Salt and the VMware Salt REST API: The enterprise-grade layer

VMware Salt is an API-driven, database-backed platform used to provide compliance, configuration drift detection and remediation for Windows, Linux and containerized kubernetes-based workloads.  VMware Salt provides full role-based access control (RBAC), a web GUI for centralized management and reporting, and support for multi-node and multi-region deployments.  VMware Salt is available for VCF as an Advanced Service (licensed add-on).

The VMware Salt REST API is the REST interface exposed by the VMware Salt server, often referred to as the Salt RaaS server. It does everything the open-source Salt API does — triggering core Salt functions — and adds endpoints to provide enterprise-grade capabilities which are supported end-to-end by Broadcom. These capabilities include programmatic control of UI-driven actions such as user management and compliance reporting, scheduled jobs, centralized job data, minion inventory, and environment health data.

Every API call is governed by the server’s RBAC, which helps ensure permissions are enforced for the user or service account making the call. VMware Salt also adds vulnerability scanning and policy-based compliance and remediation. 

Simply put, the VMware Salt enterprise API extends the open-source Salt API with full governance, reporting, and compliance.

VMware Salt for VCF Components

From VCF 9.1 onwards, Salt is also used to manage the compliance and configuration of VCF components. The Salt implementation within VCF is called VMware Salt for VCF Components and it is distinct from the VMware Salt solution for workloads.  

These capabilities are accessible from the VCF Operations console under Configuration Management and Security Posture Management. 

The difference between VMware Salt and VMware Salt for VCF Components is in the endpoints – VMware Salt endpoints are for customer workloads, VMware Salt for VCF Component endpoints are for VCF components only.

VMware Salt for VCF Components is built into VMware Cloud Foundation architecture and supports a single Salt master per VCF instance. VMware Salt for VCF Components is a fleet-level component and a single instance is shared across a VCF fleet. Therefore, the total number of Salt masters in a fleet is equal to the number of VCF instances in that fleet.

The VMware Salt for VCF control-plane is deployed as a set of containerized services on the VCF services runtime node, which is a dedicated hosting platform for the VCF management services cluster. 

VMware Salt for VCF components API: The VCF-specific configuration API

The more recent addition introduced with VCF 9.1.1 is the VMware Salt for VCF components API.  Built on VMware Salt for VCF Components, this API is designed specifically for programmatically managing configuration and compliance settings across the VCF stack, including vCenter, NSX, SDDC Manager, ESX, and other components. It uses native Salt constructs to implement and maintain desired state consistently across VCF components, exposing more than 300 built-in configuration settings. The VMware Salt for VCF components API specifically targets configuration management of the VCF stack including drift assessment and remediation at scale. 

VCF Operations continues to retain the UI console for managing configuration and compliance, while the VMware Salt for VCF components API offers a programmatic alternative, ideal for automating configuration management at scale. 

Integrating VMware Salt natively into the VCF stack transforms infrastructure management from a reactive, manual burden into an agile, self-healing execution plane. By pairing Salt’s event-driven architecture and declarative state enforcement with VCF’s unified hybrid cloud model, organizations achieve unprecedented operational speed and continuous compliance at scale. 

Instead of relying on slow UI workflows or custom scripts, operators can programmatically declare desired states across thousands of hosts, detect configuration drift in real time, and trigger automated remediation within seconds. Salt acts as the foundational engine that elevates VCF from a bare hyperconverged platform to a fully modern, enterprise-ready software-defined data center capable of self-governance and rapid automated delivery.

The VMware Salt for VCF components API can be referenced from developer.broadcom.com.

The Significance of Salt in the VCF Stack

Salt delivers a unified, end-to-end automation approach that encompasses the entire data center through a single, cohesive ecosystem. By aligning Salt for VCF to core infrastructure, VMware Salt for active workloads, and the open-source Salt Project for all remaining targets, organizations can aggressively eliminate tool sprawl and consolidate their configuration management strategy.

Instead of juggling multiple specialized automation and configuration management platforms, organizations can confidently consolidate their data center tooling to Salt, driving efficiency and unified control from end to end.

This comprehensive approach reduces operational complexity, lowers total cost of ownership, and provides seamless, centralized control across every layer of the enterprise IT landscape.

Summary

The open-source Salt Project provides the core engine and a basic API for remote execution and configuration management — free, powerful, but without enterprise governance. 

VMware Salt provides an enterprise platform with a web UI, centralized reporting, RBAC, compliance features, and a broader REST API that covers these capabilities for customer workloads. 

The VMware Salt for VCF components API is a specialized interface for managing configuration across the VCF stack at scale and leverages an embedded deployment of Salt in the VCF components. VCF 9.1.1 now provides the option to administer compliance and configuration management programmatically from the VMware Salt for VCF Components API.

Each of the three layers discussed here builds on the one before it. The open-source API is the foundation; the VMware Salt REST API provides a commercial enterprise-grade general-purpose interface for workloads, and the VMware Salt for VCF components API is used for VCF-specific configuration management. These iterations of Salt describe different sets of capabilities and are not to be confused with each other.

The VMware Salt for VCF Components API, introduced in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1.1, establishes a centralized, programmatic API interface that exposes native Salt constructs over REST APIs. This powerful capability elevates infrastructure management from manual tasks across the VCF stack, delivering the speed and agility required for modern operations.

item.title: AI時代のプライベートクラウド多層防御： VMware Cloud Foundation®で実現する仮想基盤の堅牢化とリスク低減策（第1回）
item.dc:creator: byungji kwon
item.description:
近年、生成AIをはじめとするフロンティアAI技術の進化は、ビジネスの効率化だけでなく、サイバーセキュリティの領域にも劇的な変化をもたらしています。防御側がAIを活用する一方で、攻撃者もAIを用いた高度な脆弱性探索や攻撃コードの自動生成を行うようになっています。本ブログシリーズでは、全2回にわたり「AI時代のセキュリティ対策」をテーマに、インフラのあらゆる階層で脅威を食い止める「多層防御」の実践的なアプローチを解説します。 ーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーー 第1回（本記事）：AI時代のプライベートクラウド多層防御、VMware Cloud Foundation®で実現する仮想基盤の堅牢化とリスク低減策 プライベートクラウド環境における「多層防御」の重要性と、最新のVMware Cloud Foundation® (VCF) を活用したインフラ基盤における「7つの防御層」の実装ポイントを解説します。 第2回：仮想パッチを用いたセキュリティパッチ適用までの「猶予期間」の消滅 vDefendによる「分散IDS/IPS」およびVMware® Avi™ Load Balancer WAFを用いた攻撃遮断の技術解説、およびダウンタイム不要・運用コスト削減のメリットについてお届けします。 ーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーー 1. AI時代のセキュリティ対策の心構え：フロンティアAIから学んだ教訓 AI時代におけるセキュリティの最大の変更点は、これまでの「リスク評価（トリアージ）」や「対策の猶予期間」といった前提条件が通用しなくなっている点にあります。Broadcomが実施したフロンティアAIモデルを用いたコードテストの成果からは、以下の深刻な教訓が明らかになっています。 ■ 攻撃の連鎖による「トリアージ（優先順位付け）」概念の崩壊 従来のセキュリティ運用では、発見された脆弱性をリスクの高さに応じて分類し、低リスクのものは対応を後回しにする優先順位付け（トリアージ）が一般的でした。しかし、高度なAIは「人間が一生かけても気づかないような、コードの遠く離れた場所にある要素同士の相関すらも見抜く」能力を持っています。その結果、2〜3個の「低リスクな問題」を組み合わせ・連鎖させて、1つの「致命的な攻撃パス」を作り出すことができるようになりました。これにより、「リスクの低いものは後回し」というこれまでのトリアージ概念は通用しなくなっています。 ■ 「猶予期間」の消滅 これまでは、脆弱性が公開されてから実際にそれを悪用するコードが作成されるまでに、数週間から数ヶ月の「猶予期間」がありました。しかし、AIの導入によって、このプロセスは「数週間」から「ほぼリアルタイム」に短縮されています。防御側の勝ち筋は、選別の正確さではなく、「パッチ適用の速度」や「即座に通信を遮断・制御できる能力」にかかっています。 このような状況下では、アプリケーションやミドルウェアを意識したうえで、それらが稼働するインフラ（仮想基盤）そのものの重要性を再認識し、ハードニング（要塞化）を徹底する「内部防御」および「多層防御」が極めて重要になります。 ■ 拡大する「保護すべき対象」 フロンティアAIの進化によって「攻撃の連鎖」や「全自動攻撃」が現実のものとなる中、企業がセキュリティ面で考慮すべき領域は劇的に拡大しています。サイバーセキュリティを取り巻く環境の変化に伴い、保護すべき対象はこれまでの「オンプレミス単一環境」から、「マルチクラウド」、そして「エッジ・プライベートAI基盤」へと広がっています。 このような保護対象の拡大は、攻撃者の手法が日々巧妙化していることに起因しています。攻撃側の変化・進化に合わせて、企業に求められるサイバーセキュリティ対策にも必然的に高度化が求められており、その変遷は大きく以下の3つのフェーズに分けることができます。 ・一般的に従来求められてきたサイバーセキュリティ：オンプレミス単一環境（境界型防御） 保護対象がオンプレミスの単一境界に限られ、境界に対する直接攻撃を防ぐ対策が主流でした。防御までの猶予期間も3ヶ月以上あり、境界型の防御手法で一定の対応が可能でした。 ・フロンティアAI登場前のサイバーセキュリティ：マルチクラウドへの拡張と横移動への対策 保護対象がマルチクラウドへ拡張し、境界突破後に内部で潜伏・感染を広げる攻撃が急増しました。対応猶予が3ヶ月以内に縮小する中、分散F/WやNDR等を活用した内部監視・防御策が必要となりました。 ・フロンティアAI登場後のサイバーセキュリティ：エッジ・プライベートAI基盤を含む全方位の保護 重要なデータを扱うエッジ・プライベートAI基盤へと対象が広がり、猶予なしの全自動攻撃が発生しています。高度な多層防御に加え、EDRやクリーンルーム等を連携させた迅速な復旧体制が不可欠です。   2. プライベートクラウドにおける堅牢化のポイント：多層防御によるダメージコントロール 仮想基盤におけるセキュリティ対策は、単一の壁を作るのではなく、複数の防御層を重ねることで、侵入防止と万が一侵入された際のダメージコントロールを両立させる「多層防御」が基本となります。VMware vSphere® 環境において実装すべき7つの防御層の具体策を以下にご紹介します。 ■ 多層防御によるダメージコントロール（7階層） 第1層 経路の適正運用 【概要】 North-South の経路制限・侵入防止・侵入検知 プライベートクラウドにおける「第1層」は、外部ネットワークと内部仮想基盤を結ぶ境界線、すなわち North-South（南北）トラフィック の防御を担います。ここでの目的は、基盤を管理する「心臓部」をインターネットの脅威から物理的・論理的に隔離し、許可された管理者のみが安全にアクセスできる経路を確立することです。 1. 管理インターフェースの完全隔離 VMware vCenter® … Continued
